note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure.
  - 2–3 days of wheezing and feeling short of breath, worse with walking/exertion.
  - Cough present; no phlegm; no hemoptysis.
  - Self-reported “fever,” but measured temperature 37°C.
  - Sometimes finds it difficult to complete sentences; currently feels well at rest.
  - No clear trigger identified; clinician discussed possible pollen or viral infection as causes.
- Symptom timeline and progression.
  - Onset 2–3 days ago; ongoing. Limited ability to walk to work; working from home/sick leave.
- ENT symptoms (as applicable): throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face), ear/neck symptoms.
  - No throat tightness/closing reported.
  - No voice change reported.
  - No dysphagia/odynophagia or drooling reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms not reported (history of hay fever noted).
  - No stridor/noisy breathing reported; wheeze present.
  - Dyspnea with exertion; sometimes short of breath during speech; currently comfortable at rest.
  - No facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling reported.
  - No ear pain/hearing changes; no neck pain/swelling reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments (including any prior hospital care or injection therapy).
  - Childhood asthma; required inhalers; intermittent hospital visits as a child; no ICU admissions.
  - Unclear adult episodes; patient cannot recall details.
- Allergies and current medications (mark missing dose/route/frequency as not documented).
  - Allergies: No known drug allergies.
  - Medications: Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented). Patient reports intermittent use every few weeks and with exercise; also stated he stopped asthma medication 3–4 years ago (conflict noted).
  - No regular hay fever medication.
- Any relevant social context (e.g., accompaniment/supervision).
  - Lives with partner. Works as an engineer. Non-smoker. Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution (e.g., lips, tongue, uvula, face) if stated.
  - None reported/observed.
- Airway/breathing descriptors if stated (e.g., stridor, work of breathing).
  - Reports wheeze and exertional dyspnea; able to converse during consult; currently feels well at rest. No stridor reported.
- Mental status and associated features (e.g., dizziness, syncope) if stated.
  - Alert and conversational; no dizziness/syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings only if mentioned; otherwise note “Not recorded.”
  - Temperature self-reported 37°C. No other vitals/exam recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient (if stated).
  - Not stated.

Assessment:
- Asthma exacerbation in adult with atopic history (hay fever, eczema) and prior childhood asthma.
  - Justification: 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnea, cough; sometimes difficulty completing sentences; currently stable at rest; temperature 37°C; history of asthma with prior inhaler use.
  - Possible triggers discussed: pollen exposure vs viral infection.
  - Conflict noted: Patient states he stopped asthma meds 3–4 years ago but also reports “normal” intermittent salbutamol use every few weeks and with exercise.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Prescribed peak flow meter and spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate use.
  - Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (via spacer when available).
  - Start a regular over-the-counter antihistamine (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Specific instructions provided to patient/caregiver:
  - Record peak flow values morning and evening for the next week.
  - Arrange a follow-up review in about one week to review peak flow and consider additional controller medication.
  - Pharmacist to show correct spacer technique and peak flow use.
- Escalation criteria/red flags:
  - Call the clinic immediately if temperature becomes high or wheezing worsens.
- Follow-up:
  - Phone review in ~1 week with recorded peak flows; potential initiation of additional inhaler therapy based on results and symptoms.
  - Ongoing management of hay fever discussed with regular antihistamine from pharmacy.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements for an acute ENT/allergy presentation:
  - Objective respiratory exam (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation), auscultation findings.
  - Peak flow baseline/personal best; current peak flow.
  - Detailed inhaler regimen (dose/strength) and technique assessment.
  - Controller therapy status (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid) and asthma action plan.
  - Environmental allergy details; vaccination status (influenza/COVID-19).
  - Quantity/expiry of reliever inhaler; access to spacer prior to visit.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Patient reported stopping asthma medications 3–4 years ago but also reported “normal” intermittent use of salbutamol every few weeks and with exercise.
- Transcript quality:
  - Minor communication gaps and unclear timing/medication details; otherwise adequate for basic assessment.
